chunks.text: Known in horticulture as the areca palm, golden cane palm, butterfly palm or bamboo palm, this species (botanically Dypsis lutescens, with Chrysalidocarpus lutescens used as an older or alternative name) is native to Madagascar but has been planted so widely that it now appears, often naturalised, from the Andaman Islands and Thailand to Réunion, Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Canary Islands and southern Florida. It is a clustering palm, producing several smooth, cane-like, bamboo-ringed stems from a single base, reaching anywhere from about 3.7 to 9 metres tall outdoors (considerably less in a pot). The arching pinnate fronds, 1.6–2 metres long, carry 40–60 pairs of narrow leaflets that start dark green and turn a yellowish-green with age — the yellow cast, echoed in the trunk and leaf stalks, is the source of both the scientific epithet lutescens ('becoming yellow') and the common name golden cane. Small yellow flowers cluster at the base of the crown, followed by ovoid fruit that ripens from yellow-orange to purple-black and, in places like Brazil where the palm has naturalised, feeds birds such as the great kiskadee and bananaquit. Despite its ubiquity as a houseplant and landscape screen — it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit and is often trained as a dense informal hedge — the IUCN lists the species as Near Threatened in the wild, where habitat loss in eastern Madagascar is squeezing its natural populations. Various parts of the plant have been used in traditional medicine in eastern Madagascar, and its fibre has historically been used to make fishing nets, though some tissues contain cyanide-producing compounds and are considered toxic if ingested.

chunks.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dypsis lutescens (FR309)
chunks.text: The University of Florida's extension fact sheet frames Dypsis lutescens as endemic to eastern Madagascar specifically, where it is considered endangered because its native habitat — open, seasonally flooded ('hydric') forest and riverbanks — is steadily being lost to land conversion; the ornamental trade, somewhat ironically, has made it one of the most widely cultivated palms on earth even as its wild stands shrink. The sheet describes a multi-stemmed clump 20–35 feet tall with a 10–20 foot spread, each cane 2–3 inches thick and ringed with tightly packed, variably orange, yellow or dark-green leaf scars; fronds run 6–8 feet long, with leaflets arranged in opposing pairs that form a visible 'V' along the central rachis. For best performance it recommends sites where average annual lows stay around 35–40°F, full sun to partial shade, consistently moist but well-drained soil, and planting during the summer rainy season so roots can establish before cooler weather. Yellowing fronds, a hallmark of the species, can intensify with strong sun or nutrient deficiency and can be moderated with light shading and regular fertilising. In the landscape it is most often used as an accent specimen or, planted in clusters roughly 10 feet apart, as an informal screening hedge; growers are advised to prune away lower fronds periodically both to show off the attractive ringed stems and to reduce the risk of fungal or insect problems building up in old foliage.
